subtype: Approach: setting small distances as goals [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Nidhi watched the others race lengths and felt slow. "One width," she told herself. She swam it, touched the wall and grinned, and wrote a 1 in her swim book.
The next Monday she managed two widths, gasping but done. A 2 went in the book.
By the third Monday it was four. Her brother Samir clicked the stopwatch at the wall and said, "Whoa." Nidhi did not care that the others were still faster. She turned back a page and looked at the row of numbers, climbing.

qa.q: How many widths did Nidhi swim on the third Monday?
qa.a: She swam four widths on the third Monday.

qa.q: What was Nidhi feeling on the first Monday as she watched the others?
qa.a: Slow and a little discouraged, which is why she gave herself just one width to do.

qa.q: What other approach could keep Nidhi motivated if progress stalls, and why?
qa.a: She could swim with a friend at her speed and cheer each other's widths, since a shared count helps when her own numbers stop rising.

qa.q: How does Samir see Nidhi's progress?
qa.a: Samir is impressed, as his "Whoa" shows, because he has watched the widths grow week by week.

grounding: A girl who feels slow sets small distance goals, one width then two, and counts her progress each week.

subtype: Approach: setting small distances as goals [Revision]
passage: Vandana, you think you're the slowest in your swimming class? Let your Parveen Nani tell you something. When I learned, at a pool in Lucknow, all the girls were faster than me. I felt like a buffalo among fish. Then one day I stopped comparing. I said, "This week, I will swim one width without stopping." That was all. It took four tries. The next week: two widths. Then three. I kept a little chart on the back of my notebook, and every Saturday I wrote the number. By the end of summer I had forty ticks on that chart. I was still not the fastest. But I could see, every week, that I was faster than me.

qa.q: What did Parveen write on the chart every Saturday?
qa.a: Parveen wrote the number of widths.

qa.q: How did young Parveen feel among the faster girls?
qa.a: Young Parveen felt slow and discouraged, like a buffalo among fish.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: The turning point was dropping the comparison and aiming for one width, because a small goal could be reached and counted.

qa.q: How might the other girls in the class have seen young Parveen?
qa.a: They may have noticed Parveen getting steadily stronger and gained some respect for that quiet progress.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling slow as a girl learning to swim, setting goals of one width and then two, and counting progress each week.

subtype: Approach: setting small distances as goals [Revision]
passage: Nandini's swimming slot at the municipal pool was only thirty minutes, and the lanes were so crowded that she spent half of it waiting. She felt she was getting nowhere. On Monday she told her friend Vidya, "I'm going to stop trying to swim fast and just try for one full width." In the next slot she swam one width without stopping, dodging a man doing backstroke. On Thursday she tried two. She kept the count on a card in her bag: Week 1: one width. Week 2: two. Week 3: three, even though the lane was packed. Vidya started keeping a card too. "It's not about how fast," Nandini told her. "It's about the number going up."

qa.q: How long was Nandini's swimming slot?
How did Nandini feel before she changed her goal?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and stuck, as if she was getting nowhere in the crowded pool.

qa.q: What else could Nandini try when the lanes are packed?
qa.a: She could use the waiting time to practise breathing at the wall, so no minute of the short slot is wasted.

qa.q: How does Nandini's plan look to Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya sees it working and starts her own card, so it seems useful and encouraging to her.

grounding: It shows a girl who feels slow setting small goals of one width, then two, and counting her widths each week.
